My Role: Developing State Growth Models

 Education as a process (growth) instead of a destination (status).
 Growth/Value-Added Model Selection: Important but the easiest
 step (You have a growth/value-added model, now what).
 Identifying stakeholder groups who will make use (who we want to
 make use) of these data: Parents, teachers, principals, policy
 makers, . . . .
 The data can tell a thousand stories: Crafting data narratives that
 foster educational improvement.
 The data do not speak for themselves.
 My role: Educate state clients about growth and help them develop a
 new vocabulary that enables conversations about the progress of
 students through the education system.

Developing a Successful Growth Model

 In the states demonstrating success in implementing student growth
 models, one commonality stands out: Commitment to the growth
 model by three key groups within any department of education:
 Directors of Measurement/Assessment.
 Directors of Accountability.
 Directors of Information-Technology.
 Measurement/Assessment specialists understand the state
 assessments and will need to be able to understand and explain
 growth data derived from those assessments.
 Accountability directors will be involved in the use of these data,
 particularly as they pertain to accountability initiatives.
 CIOs/IT directors will often be tasked will helping to disseminate the
 results of the growth model.
 These directors become mavens for the work to others within their
 organization that reach out to the diverse range of stakeholders.

Summary

 Growth models can fundamentally change conversations (for the
 better) about education.
 Orchestrating these changes requires broad ownership and
 adoption of the growth model within a DOE.
 Growth model adoption is a two to three year process: Changing
 perceptions of education as a process instead of a destination takes
 time.
 Leading states like Massachusetts and Colorado have been mavens
 illustrating how data can be turned into information.
